title: The Bronze at Eighteenth Street
premise: George Pullman put up a bronze statue of a battle from 1812 near his door. A year later soldiers came to Chicago again, this time to stop his own workers. Who gets to tell history?

opening.text:
JAUNT: THE BRONZE AT EIGHTEENTH STREET. It is a Monday afternoon in November 1904, at the corner of Eighteenth Street and Prairie Avenue.

There are four stops around one street corner. Under the street is an old battlefield. Near it stands a bronze statue that tells a story about the battle. Next is the house of the man who paid for the statue. Last is the house that stared back at him. At every stop, ask: what really happened, and who chose how we remember it?

Start where the street starts, on the ground where the battle was fought.

stops.text: This is Prairie Avenue at Eighteenth Street. Long ago, before the houses, there were sand hills here by the lake. On 15 August 1812 the Battle of Fort Dearborn was fought across them. The people who died lay in the sand for four years. For a hundred years a big cottonwood tree marked the place. Now look at the street in 1904. There is brick, granite stone and gas lamps. A teacher is bringing her class to see the sights. The battle was 92 years ago, and now it is a lesson. Who wrote the lesson? Walk east along Eighteenth Street to the statue.

stage.caption: A teacher leads a line of children along Eighteenth Street to the statue.

stops.text: Here is the statue. George Pullman paid for it in 1893 and put it near his front door. It shows Black Partridge, a Potawatomi chief, saving Margaret Helm, an army officer's wife. It is exciting, but it may never have happened. Some historians think the story was made up later. They say Mrs. Helm rode her horse to the lake shore and found safety there. The artist did not study the real people of 1812. One historian says his figures looked more like a Wild West show. The teacher is reading the sign out loud. Now look at the house behind the statue.

stage.caption: The teacher reads to her class at the foot of the statue. The children look up at it.

stops.text: This is 1729 Prairie, the Pullman house. Mr. Pullman built railroad sleeping cars. South of the city he built a whole town for his workers, and they paid him rent. In 1894 he cut their pay but did not lower the rent. So the workers went on strike. Here is the part the statue does not tell. A year after the statue went up, army soldiers came to Chicago to stop the strike against Mr. Pullman. Pullman died in 1897, and his house will be torn down in 1922. Cross Prairie to the house that stared at his.

stage.caption: Two working men carrying tools stop on the far sidewalk to look at the Pullman house. Then they walk on.

stops.text: This is the Glessner house, across the corner from Pullman. Pullman did not like it. He said he did not know what he had done to have "that thing staring me in the face" every time he went out his door. When he died, his family was afraid robbers, or angry workers, might dig up his grave. So they buried him in a box sealed in a big block of concrete, with steel rails on top. One historian says we don't really know if every part of that story is true. That is the lesson of this corner. Bronze, stone and concrete are on top. Under all of it is the old sand.

stage.caption: The class walks past the Glessner house on its way home. The teacher looks back at the Pullman house.

legs.story: East along Eighteenth Street to the statue by the Pullman fence.
Back around the Pullman yard to the front of the house on Prairie Avenue.
Across the corner to the Glessner house, facing Pullman's door.

endings.text: The walk ends here. In 1904 the statue still stands at Eighteenth Street, telling its story one way. Some historians doubt the rescue ever happened. Pullman lies under his concrete. People still learn about the strike he broke. The ground under this corner still holds the sand of 1812. A statue tells you who paid for it. To learn the rest, you have to dig.

keepsake.title: The Monument Question
keepsake.text: A card about the 1893 statue at Eighteenth Street and the history behind it. It is a made-up keepsake, not an object from history.

evidence.text: The Battle of Fort Dearborn occurred in the area that is now the northern section of the street.

The dead of 15 August 1812 'lay in the sand, half buried where they were killed, until 1816'; the site, in the sand hills of the lake shore between 16th and 18th streets near the north-east corner of 18th and Prairie (accounts differ), 'was marked by for over a century by a large cottonwood tree'. A Tribune article of 1900 says the Pullman house 'stands about where the massacre took place'.
evidence.locator: The post's paragraphs on the site, its tree and the Tribune of 1900.

evidence.text: The Bronze at Eighteenth Street: the day, Monday 21 November 1904, the hour and the order of the walk are this jaunt's framing, chosen because the stories meet on it (three days after Arthur Caton's death, a Monday of the Reading Class, before Kimball's death in December). No visit on that day is asserted.

The Bronze at Eighteenth Street: who is seen at each stop, where they stand, what they do and when are reconstructed. People with cards in the town play themselves; people the town has no card for (and the unnamed servants, callers and passers-by) are unnamed figures in period dress, and no likeness is claimed. No word anyone says is asserted.

George Pullman commissioned Carl Rohl-Smith's bronze of the Potawatomi chief Black Partridge saving Margaret Helm, the wife of an army officer, placed in 1893 'near the intersection of Prairie Avenue and 18th Street'.
evidence.locator: The monument article's history; the cemetery post's paragraph on the 1893 statue, removed in 1931.

evidence.text: 'Some historians regard the incident as the product of romantic imagination instead of eyewitness testimony, stating that Margaret Helm was not the beneficiary of Black Partridge's dramatic rescue. In fact, before the battle turned into a massacre, Mrs. Helm rode her horse to the shore of Lake Michigan where she found refuge.'

Rohl-Smith obtained his models at Fort Sheridan, where he met survivors of Wounded Knee, whom he described as 'Indians of the most untamed sort'. His figures 'may have owed more to Buffalo Bill Cody's Wild West Show than to actual research.'
In 1894 Pullman cut his workers' wages, but 'he didn't reduce the rent in Pullman', his company town; he 'died of a heart attack' on 19 October 1897.
evidence.locator: The biography's paragraphs on the strike and his death.

evidence.text: 'a year after the statue's dedication', the Seventh Cavalry, 'which had fought Indians so fiercely at Little Big Horn and Wounded Knee, came to Chicago to quell the Pullman riots of 1894.'

Pullman's firm raised Chicago buildings out of the mud 'on average six feet without causing them any damage'; his first sleeping car 'was finished in 1864'; Lincoln's body went home to Springfield in a sleeper while 'hundreds of thousands of people lined the route in homage'.
evidence.locator: The biography's paragraphs on building-raising, the sleeping car and Lincoln's funeral.

evidence.text: George M. Pullman Residence, 1729 S. Prairie Avenue: razed 1922.
George Pullman, across the street, complained of the Glessner house: 'I do not know what I have ever done to have that thing staring me in the face every time I go out of my door'.

Fearing his body would be dug up, the family had him buried in a 'lead-lined mahogany coffin, which was then sealed inside a block of concrete', under steel rails 'bolted together at right angles', at Graceland Cemetery. An 1897 New York Times account gives a 'lead-lined box wrapped in tar paper' and 'an inch of asphaltum'; behind it, 'a lot of high-profile grave robberies lately' and the fear that 'some of the employees weren't quite done getting revenge'. The historian Adam Selzer: 'Whether it's true or not, we don't really know.'
evidence.locator: The biography's paragraph on the burial; the WTTW piece on the grave.

evidence.text: Glessner built at the corner of Eighteenth Street and Prairie Avenue, diagonally opposite Pullman's mansion.
